title: Reward Inflation: A Healthy Stimulus for Reinforcement Learning
claim: Gradually scaling rewards boosts nominal performance, upweights recent transitions, and sustains gradient signals relative to baseline or deflation.
layout: 4 panels in a row, left-to-right, color-coded curves with slope annotations
description: A single-row figure with four line-plot panels. (a) Performance Growth Over Time: episode reward against steps up to 3M, with a blue Nominal curve rising to about 28000 and a dashed teal Real curve flattening near 16000, both with shaded bands. (b) Inflation Rate: a flat line at 0.02 on top, and below it an Inflation Level curve rising from 1.0 to about 1.8. (c) TD Error against transition age, 10K to 100K steps, with three downward-sloping curves. Blue Inflation (2%) has slope -6.06, gray Baseline (0%) has slope -4.83, and red Deflation (-2%) has slope -3.96. (d) Gradient norm over training for policy π_φ and critic Q_θ. The blue inflation curve grows large while gray and red stay low. Blue, gray and red encode inflation, baseline and deflation throughout.
caption: (a) The nominal and real performance growth over training time under 2% inflation. (b) The inflation rate and inflation level I(g) over the training time. (c) The TD error w.r.t. the transition age in replay buffer, across the inflation rates. (d) The changes of gradient norms during training.
abstract: Reward serves as the primary learning signal in reinforcement learning (RL). However, while reward magnitudes are typically held fixed throughout training, their temporal modulation remains underexplored. In this paper, we propose reward inflation, a gradual scaling of rewards over the course of training, and show that it can act as a healthy stimulus for RL. Theoretically, reward inflation induces an implicit recency weighting that upweights recent transitions during policy updates, enabling faster adaptation. We further show that reward inflation suppresses the emergence of dormant neurons by sustaining gradient signals as the policy saturates, suggesting a possible contribution to plasticity preservation. Empirical results on ALE games and MuJoCo tasks corroborate these findings, showing that an appropriate level of reward inflation benefits a broad range of tasks. Finally, we introduce Fed, an adaptive variant that adjusts the inflation level on the fly, and find that it often improves upon fixed inflation. Source code is available at https://github.com/northadventure/RewardInflation.
